summary.text: For the candidate linear-recurrence sequence, the proof studies the error term \(D_n=L_{n-1}^2-L_nL_{n-2}\), deriving \(D_{m+5}=4D_{m+3}+D_{m+2}\) and using its initial values together with the growth bound \(L_{n+1}\ge 3L_n\) to show \(1\le D_n\le L_{n-2}\). These inequalities make \(L_n\) exactly \(\lceil L_{n-1}^2/L_{n-2}\rceil-1\), so induction identifies the originally defined sequence with the linear-recurrence sequence.

full_proof.text:
Let \((b_n)_{n\ge 0}\) be the sequence given by the original definition. Thus
\[
b_0=4,\qquad b_1=16,
\]
and, once \(b_n,b_{n+1}\) have been defined, \(b_{n+2}\) is the greatest integer satisfying
\[
\frac{b_{n+2}}{b_{n+1}}<\frac{b_{n+1}}{b_n}.
\]
All terms that occur below are positive. Multiplying the displayed inequality by the positive number \(b_{n+1}b_n\), the condition on a candidate integer \(q=b_{n+2}\) is
\[
q<\frac{b_{n+1}^2}{b_n}.
\]
For every real number \(r\), the greatest integer strictly less than \(r\) is \(\lceil r\rceil-1\), whether or not \(r\) itself is an integer. Consequently the original definition is equivalently
\[
b_{n+2}=\left\lceil\frac{b_{n+1}^2}{b_n}\right\rceil-1. \tag{1}
\]
We prove that this sequence satisfies
\[
b_0=4,\quad b_1=16,\quad b_2=63,\qquad
b_n=4b_{n-1}-b_{n-3}\quad(n\ge 3). \tag{2}
\]
This will also prove the claimed generating function.

Define an auxiliary integer sequence \((L_n)_{n\ge0}\) by
\[
L_0=4,\qquad L_1=16,\qquad L_2=63,
\]
and
\[
L_{m+3}=4L_{m+2}-L_m\qquad(m\ge0). \tag{3}
\]
The first few terms are
\[
4,16,63,248,976,3841,\ldots.
\]
Our goal is to prove that the nonlinear extremal recurrence (1) produces exactly \(L_n\).

We first establish positivity and a useful growth estimate:
\[
L_n\ge0\quad\text{and}\quad L_{n+1}\ge3L_n
\qquad(n\ge0). \tag{4}
\]
We use strong induction. For \(n=0,1,2\), this follows directly:
\[
16\ge3\cdot4,\qquad 63\ge3\cdot16,
\qquad 248=4\cdot63-4\ge3\cdot63,
\]
and all the terms involved are nonnegative.

Suppose now that the assertions have already been proved through index \(m+2\). By (3),
\[
L_{m+3}=4L_{m+2}-L_m.
\]
The induction hypotheses give
\(L_{m+2}\ge3L_{m+1}\ge9L_m\ge0\), so in particular
\(4L_{m+2}-L_m\ge0\). Thus \(L_{m+3}\ge0\). Also
\[
L_{m+4}=4L_{m+3}-L_{m+1}.
\]
It therefore suffices, in order to prove \(L_{m+4}\ge3L_{m+3}\), to show
\(L_{m+3}\ge L_{m+1}\). But the already established estimate
\(L_{m+3}\ge3L_{m+2}\), together with nonnegativity and
\(L_{m+2}\ge3L_{m+1}\), gives this immediately. This completes the strong induction and proves (4). In fact every \(L_n\) is strictly positive: \(L_0=4\), and repeated use of \(L_{n+1}\ge3L_n\) gives \(L_n\ge4\) for all \(n\).

The key issue is now to determine precisely where the quotient
\(L_{n+1}^2/L_n\) lies relative to consecutive integers. For \(n\ge2\), define
\[
D_n=L_{n-1}^2-L_nL_{n-2}. \tag{5}
\]
Direct calculation gives the three initial values
\[
D_2=16^2-63\cdot4=4,
\]
\[
D_3=63^2-248\cdot16=1,
\]
and
\[
D_4=248^2-976\cdot63=16. \tag{6}
\]
The sequence \(D_n\) satisfies
\[
D_{m+5}=4D_{m+3}+D_{m+2}\qquad(m\ge0). \tag{7}
\]
To see this, use (3) at three successive indices:
\[
L_{m+3}=4L_{m+2}-L_m,
\]
\[
L_{m+4}=4L_{m+3}-L_{m+1},
\]
\[
L_{m+5}=4L_{m+4}-L_{m+2}.
\]
Substituting these identities into
\[
D_{m+5}=L_{m+4}^2-L_{m+5}L_{m+3}
\]
and expanding and collecting terms gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
D_{m+5}
&=4\bigl(L_{m+2}^2-L_{m+3}L_{m+1}\bigr)
  +\bigl(L_{m+1}^2-L_{m+2}L_m\bigr)\\
&=4D_{m+3}+D_{m+2},
\end{aligned}
\]
as asserted.

We next prove the decisive two-sided bound
\[
1\le D_n\le L_{n-2}\qquad(n\ge2). \tag{8}
\]
Again we use strong induction. The cases \(n=2,3,4\) follow from (6):
\[
1\le D_2=4\le L_0=4,
\]
\[
1\le D_3=1\le L_1=16,
\]
and
\[
1\le D_4=16\le L_2=63.
\]
For the induction step, let \(n=m+5\). Applying (7) and the induction hypotheses at \(m+3\) and \(m+2\) gives
\[
D_{m+5}=4D_{m+3}+D_{m+2}\ge4\cdot1+1\ge1.
\]
For the upper bound, the same induction hypotheses give
\[
D_{m+5}\le4L_{m+1}+L_m. \tag{9}
\]
We must compare the right-hand side with \(L_{m+3}\). By (3),
\[
L_{m+3}=4L_{m+2}-L_m.
\]
The growth estimates (4) imply
\(L_{m+2}\ge3L_{m+1}\) and \(L_{m+1}\ge3L_m\). In particular,
\[
\begin{aligned}
L_{m+3}-(4L_{m+1}+L_m)
 &=4(L_{m+2}-L_{m+1})-2L_m\\
 &\ge 8L_{m+1}-2L_m\\
 &\ge0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Together with (9), this proves
\(D_{m+5}\le L_{m+3}=L_{(m+5)-2}\), completing the induction and proving (8).

Apply (8) with index \(n+2\). From the definition (5),
\[
D_{n+2}=L_{n+1}^2-L_{n+2}L_n,
\]
so (8) says
\[
1\le L_{n+1}^2-L_{n+2}L_n\le L_n. \tag{10}
\]
Equivalently,
\[
L_{n+2}L_n+1\le L_{n+1}^2
   \le L_{n+2}L_n+L_n. \tag{11}
\]
Since \(L_n>0\), division by \(L_n\) yields
\[
L_{n+2}<\frac{L_{n+1}^2}{L_n}\le L_{n+2}+1. \tag{12}
\]
The least integer greater than or equal to a real number lying in this half-open interval is exactly \(L_{n+2}+1\). Therefore
\[
\left\lceil\frac{L_{n+1}^2}{L_n}\right\rceil-1=L_{n+2}. \tag{13}
\]
Notice that (10) also handles the possible divisibility endpoint: if the upper bound is an equality, then the quotient in (12) is exactly \(L_{n+2}+1\), and its ceiling is still \(L_{n+2}+1\).

For completeness, the same conclusion can be seen using only integer division. For positive integers \(X,Y\),
\[
\left\lceil\frac XY\right\rceil=\left\lfloor\frac{X+Y-1}{Y}\right\rfloor.
\]
Taking \(X=L_{n+1}^2\) and \(Y=L_n\), inequalities (11) give
\[
(L_{n+2}+1)L_n\le L_{n+1}^2+L_n-1
 <(L_{n+2}+2)L_n.
\]
Thus the integer quotient of \(L_{n+1}^2+L_n-1\) by \(L_n\) is exactly \(L_{n+2}+1\), which is again (13).

We now identify the original sequence. We prove by strong induction that
\[
b_n=L_n\qquad(n\ge0). \tag{14}
\]
For \(n=0,1\), this is true by definition. At \(n=2\), formula (1) gives
\[
b_2=\left\lceil\frac{16^2}{4}\right\rceil-1=64-1=63=L_2.
\]
More generally, suppose \(b_j=L_j\) for all \(j<n+2\). Then in particular
\(b_n=L_n\) and \(b_{n+1}=L_{n+1}\). Using first the original recurrence (1), then (13), we obtain
\[
b_{n+2}
 =\left\lceil\frac{b_{n+1}^2}{b_n}\right\rceil-1
 =\left\lceil\frac{L_{n+1}^2}{L_n}\right\rceil-1
 =L_{n+2}.
\]
This completes the induction. Hence the original extremal sequence is precisely \(L\). In particular,
\[
b_0=4,\qquad b_1=16,\qquad b_2=63,
\]
and for every \(n\ge3\), equation (3) becomes
\[
b_n=4b_{n-1}-b_{n-3}.
\]
This proves the stated linear-recurrence form of the conjecture.

It remains to translate the recurrence into the claimed generating function. Let
\[
B(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}b_nx^n
\]
be the ordinary generating function, regarded as a formal power series. Consider
\((1-4x+x^3)B(x)\). Its constant coefficient is \(b_0=4\). Its coefficient of \(x\) is
\[
b_1-4b_0=16-16=0,
\]
and its coefficient of \(x^2\) is
\[
b_2-4b_1=63-64=-1.
\]
For every \(n\ge3\), the coefficient of \(x^n\) is
\[
b_n-4b_{n-1}+b_{n-3}=0
\]
by the recurrence just proved. Therefore, as an identity of formal power series,
\[
(1-4x+x^3)B(x)=4-x^2.
\]
The polynomial \(1-4x+x^3\) has constant term \(1\), so it is invertible as a formal power series. Dividing by it gives
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle B(x)=\frac{4-x^2}{1-4x+x^3}}.
\]
Thus the sequence arising from the original, non-alternating extremal consecutive-ratio definition has exactly the conjectured generating function.
